about.title: San Bernardino Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: Traffic in San Bernardino moves through a handful of busy channels: the SR-210 and I-215 freeways, and surface streets like E Highland Avenue and W Baseline Street that carry people to work, school, and home. In 2025, public records show 1,380 injury collisions in the city, with 2,068 people hurt and 32 lives lost. Collisions here tend to cluster on Friday evenings between 5 and 7 p.m., when the commute is heaviest. If you were one of those injured, the days after a crash can feel scattered. Medical bills arrive before you know who is paying. An adjuster from the other driver's insurer may call asking for a recorded statement. You do not have to give one. LawProactive exists to take one item off that list. Tell us what happened, and we connect you at no charge with an independent personal injury attorney serving San Bernardino County who works on contingency. There is no fee unless your case produces a recovery, and the decision to hire anyone stays entirely with you.

whyChoose.title: Why San Bernardino Drivers Use LawProactive

items.title: The clock matters, and it can be short
items.desc: California gives most car accident victims two years to file, but a claim involving a city, county, or Caltrans vehicle or roadway can require notice in as little as six months. Getting connected early protects that window.

items.title: Partial fault does not close the door
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still recover even if you were partly to blame; your share of fault simply reduces the amount. An attorney can push back when an insurer tries to overstate your percentage.

items.title: Free connection, contingency representation
items.desc: LawProactive charges you nothing to make the introduction. The independent attorney you speak with works on contingency, so there is no attorney fee unless your case results in a recovery.

items.question: The other driver's insurance company wants a recorded statement. Should I give one?
items.answer: You are not required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer, and it is generally wise to decline until you have spoken with an attorney. Adjusters are trained to ask questions that can be used to shift fault or minimize your injuries. Instead, focus on preserving evidence: photos of the vehicles and scene, the police report number, witness contact information, and every medical record.

items.question: I was hurt in a crash on I-215 during the Friday evening commute. Does the time or location change my claim?
items.answer: Not the legal rules, but it can affect the evidence. Freeway collisions in San Bernardino often involve multiple vehicles, CHP rather than city police reports, and traffic camera or dashcam footage that gets overwritten quickly. Reaching an attorney soon after a crash gives them a better chance to secure that footage and identify every potentially responsible party.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover for pain and suffering in California?
items.answer: For ordinary car accident claims, California places no cap on non-economic damages such as pain, suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life. What you can recover depends on the facts of your case, your medical evidence, and how fault is divided. No one can promise a particular result, but an attorney can explain how these factors apply to your situation.
